title: The Clockmaker's Winter Evening
subtitle: A slow sleep story for tonight
about: An invented story about a clockmaker repairing an old pocket watch on a snowy night. Not a true story.
text:
Welcome. This story is invented, and it is meant to be listened to slowly. There is nothing to remember and nothing to work out. If you fall asleep before the end, that is perfectly all right. The story will carry on without you.

Let your body settle into the bed. Let the weight of your head rest fully on the pillow, and let your shoulders drop away from your ears. Breathe in gently through your nose. Breathe out through your mouth, as if you were fogging a window. Once more. In, and out. Good.

Now picture a small town in the mountains, in the middle of winter. Snow has been falling since the afternoon, softly and without any wind. It settles on the roofs, on the fence posts, on the bare branches of the apple trees, and every sound in the town grows quieter because of it.

At the top of the lane there is a narrow house with a green door, and behind the house stands a little workshop built of dark wood. Over its door hangs a painted sign in the shape of a clock face. The hands on the sign have long ago faded to a soft grey, and no one in the town minds, because everyone knows who lives inside.

His name is Anselm, and he is a clockmaker. He is a tall, patient man with silver hair and round glasses, and he wears a knitted cardigan the colour of porridge. He has repaired the clocks of this town for as long as most people can remember, and he has never once been in a hurry.

This evening the snow has closed the lane, and nobody will come to the workshop until morning. Anselm does not mind. He likes evenings like this one. He puts a pot of water on the little iron stove, and he listens to it begin to hum, long before it begins to boil.

The workshop is warm. The stove glows through its small window, and the light moves slowly across the ceiling beams. Along the walls hang clocks of every size, some with painted faces, some with plain white ones, and some with no faces at all, only their quiet brass insides. They tick together, but never quite at the same moment, like rain on a roof.

Above the bench hangs a lamp with a green glass shade. Its light falls in a small, perfect circle, and within that circle everything is clear and still. Beyond it, the corners of the room soften into shadow, and the shadows are friendly, like blankets laid over furniture. Nothing in them needs your attention.

On the windowsill, curled on a folded blanket, sleeps a grey cat called Bramble. She has one white paw, and she sleeps with it tucked under her chin. Every few minutes her ear twitches, and then it grows still again. Anselm glances at her, and smiles, and turns back to his work.

On the workbench in front of him lies a small pocket watch. It belonged to a woman from the next valley, who brought it in last week wrapped in a handkerchief. She told him it had been her grandfather's, and that it had stopped many years ago, and that she did not mind if it never ran again. She only wanted it to be well.

Beside the watch lie a few small treasures: a magnifying glass with a worn wooden handle, a jar of tiny screws sorted by size, and a thimble that Anselm uses to hold his oil. Each has its own place. Each has been in that place for years, and each knows it.

Anselm lays a soft cloth on the bench, and sets the watch upon it. He lifts his glasses, and then lowers them again. He takes a tiny screwdriver from a row of tools that lie in the order of their size, and he turns it, slowly, a quarter of a turn at a time.

The back of the watch opens with a faint click. Inside, there is a small, golden world. Wheels no bigger than lentils sit beside one another. A thin spring is coiled like a sleeping snail. Tiny red jewels shine at the points where the wheels turn, and they catch the light of the stove.

Anselm breathes slowly, and looks. He has learned that a watch will tell you what is wrong, if you give it enough quiet. So he gives it quiet. He listens to the room, to the stove, to the snow against the glass, and to the soft breathing of the cat.

After a while he notices a speck of dust sitting on one of the wheels. It is so small that you could only see it by the light of a candle held at just the right angle. He takes a fine brush made from a single sable hair, and he touches it to the wheel, as lightly as a falling snowflake.

The speck lifts away. He blows once, very gently, and it drifts off into the warm air. He watches it float down toward the floor, turning slowly, and he thinks that even dust has somewhere to go in the end.

He moves on to the next wheel, and the next. With each one, he takes a little oil from a glass dish. He uses a tool so thin that it is nearly a needle, and he places one drop, no bigger than a grain of sand, where the metal meets the jewel. Then he waits, and watches the oil spread, and he is content.

The water on the stove begins to sing. Anselm rises from his stool, and his knees give their familiar little creak. He pours the water into a brown teapot, and drops in a spoonful of dried chamomile and a curl of orange peel. The steam rises in a soft, golden thread, and the whole workshop smells of summer.

He carries his cup back to the bench, and sets it where the heat will not touch the watch. He sits, and takes a sip, and feels the warmth travel slowly from his chest out to his fingertips. Everything in his body feels heavy and calm, just as the evening is heavy and calm.

Outside, the snow keeps falling. If you stood at the window, you would see it come down in large, unhurried flakes, each one turning a little, as though it had all the time in the world. They land on the sill, and on the glass, and they melt and join and slide down in thin silver lines.

Anselm returns to the watch. He lifts the tiny spring with a pair of tweezers, and he looks at it closely. He finds that it is not broken, only tired. It has simply gone a very long time without being wound, and it has forgotten how to hold its shape.

So he does the kindest thing he knows. He places the spring in a small dish, and covers it with a clean cloth, and leaves it to rest. He tells it, quietly, that there is no hurry. He tells it that it has done a good job for a great many years, and that it may take as long as it needs.

While the spring rests, Anselm turns to the other clocks. He does this every evening. He walks along the wall, and he winds each one, slowly, one after another. The brass keys make a soft clicking sound as they turn, and each clock answers with a faint, contented whirr.

As he turns each key, he counts the turns under his breath. One, and two, and three. The numbers are quiet and round, like pebbles dropped into still water. By the time he reaches the last clock, he has forgotten what he was counting, and it does not matter.

First, the tall clock by the door, whose pendulum swings like a slow, golden tide. Then the round one above the stove, with its painted blue flowers. Then the small cuckoo clock, whose little bird is asleep behind its wooden door, and who will not be woken until morning.

At every clock, Anselm pauses for a moment, and listens. He does not need to look at the time. He knows each of them as one knows the voices of old friends. This one ticks a little quickly when it is cold. That one ticks a little slowly when the air is damp. He loves them all the same.

When he reaches the window, he stops beside the cat. He lays two fingers very lightly on the top of her head, and she opens one green eye, and closes it again. The purr starts up like a tiny engine, steady and warm, and it joins the ticking of the clocks until the whole room seems to be breathing together.

He stands there for a while, and looks out at the lane. The snow has covered everything in a soft white blanket. The street lamp at the corner glows a gentle yellow, and each flake that passes through its light shines for just a moment, and then vanishes into the dark.

He thinks about the people of the town, each of them in their own warm house tonight. The baker, with flour still on her sleeves. The teacher, reading by a lamp. The old fisherman who has moved far inland and still keeps a little boat on his bookshelf. All of them are safe, and all of them are resting.

He thinks of the river beyond the town, frozen at its edges, still moving quietly in the middle. He thinks of the pine forest on the hill, where the snow lies in soft heaps along every branch. He thinks of the owls, who are awake somewhere, and who do not mind the cold.

Anselm returns to his stool, and lifts the cloth from the little dish. The spring lies quietly in the light. He takes it up again with the tweezers, and now it feels different, as though it has stretched itself in its sleep. Slowly, he fits it back into the watch, and it settles into place with a very small sound.

Next come the wheels, one by one. Each slips into its own place, as though it were going home. He closes the case, and then, with the tip of his finger, he turns the little crown, a few turns, no more. He holds the watch up to his ear, and he waits.

For a moment there is only the room. The stove, the snow, the purring of the cat. Then, from inside the watch, comes a sound so faint that you might think you imagined it. Tick. And then another. Tick. And then another, steady and small, like the heartbeat of a very young bird.

Anselm closes his eyes. He does not smile with his mouth, but with the whole of his face. The watch is running. After so many years, it is running again, and its small, bright sound blends with all the others on the walls, until he cannot tell which is which.

He sets the watch gently on its cloth, and he leaves it there. Tomorrow he will polish its case, and fit a new glass, and tie a soft ribbon through its ring. But tonight there is nothing more to do. Tonight, the watch is simply allowed to tick.

He rises, and banks the stove with a few split logs, so that it will glow through the night. He puts out the lamp over the workbench, and then the lamp by the door. The workshop does not grow dark. It grows amber, lit only by the stove and by the pale blue glow of the snow outside.

Bramble stretches, and yawns, and hops down from the windowsill. She walks across the floor with her tail held high, and she curls up on the rug in front of the stove. She tucks her white paw beneath her chin, exactly as before. Anselm covers her with a corner of his old wool blanket.

He climbs the narrow stairs to his small room beneath the roof. The stairs creak, one by one, in a gentle rhythm he knows by heart. At the top, the room is cool and quiet, and a quilt lies folded on the bed. Through the little round window, he can see the snow still falling.

On the table by the bed there is a small glass of water, and a candle in a brass holder that he does not light tonight. There is also a book he has been reading for months, one page each evening. Tonight he does not open it. The book is content to wait, as books are.

He sits on the edge of the bed, and takes off his glasses, and folds them onto the table. He slips beneath the quilt, and it is soft and heavy, and it holds him the way a calm sea holds a boat. He rests his head on the pillow, and feels it take the weight.

He thinks of his mother's kitchen, many years ago, and of the old clock that hung above the door. He remembers how its tick came through the wall when he was small, and how it told him, night after night, that everything was in order. He is that clock, now, for others.

Down below, the clocks keep ticking. You can hear them through the floorboards, a soft, steady pattern like a distant rain. Each tick is a small step, and each step is slow, and none of them is going anywhere in particular. They are only keeping the night company.

Anselm lets his breath grow long. In, and then out, slower than the one before. His hands lie open on the quilt, and his fingers feel warm and loose. He thinks of the watch, ticking in its cloth. He thinks of the spring, rested and ready. He thinks of nothing at all.

The snow keeps falling, quietly, over the roofs and the fields and the long, dark hills. It falls on the green door, and on the little sign with its faded hands. It falls on the road that no one will walk tonight, and it gently fills in every footprint, until the world is smooth and white and still.

And somewhere in the middle of all that quiet, Anselm falls asleep. His breathing is even. His face is calm. The cat is asleep by the stove, and the watch is ticking on the bench, and every clock in the workshop keeps its slow and gentle time, because there is no one left to hurry.

Now it is your turn to do just the same. Let your breathing find its own pace. Let your arms and legs grow heavy, as if they were sinking softly into the bed. Let your jaw loosen, and your forehead smooth, and your thoughts drift away like snowflakes beyond the window.

Imagine, if you like, that a clock is ticking somewhere near your bed. Each tick lets another small thought go. Tick, and a worry loosens. Tick, and a plan dissolves. Tick, and your body grows heavier and warmer, like a stone that has lain all day in the sun.

You do not need to listen anymore. The night will keep itself. The clocks will keep the time, and the snow will keep falling, and you are warm, and you are safe, and there is nothing at all left to do.

You can rest now.

Goodnight.
